title: CBAM Evidence Review
custom_excerpt: Your emissions data against the importer's actual request: product scope, installation records, embedded-emissions logic and document governance — before the buyer's deadline.
meta_title: CBAM Evidence Review for Brazilian Suppliers | Villanova ESG
meta_description: Advisory review of CBAM evidence for Brazilian suppliers: CN-code scope, installation data, embedded emissions, contract clauses and document governance against the EU importer's actual request.
html:
The CBAM definitive regime applies since 1 January 2026 (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2083). The formal obligation sits with the EU importer — but you control the operational facts the importer needs. If your product and emissions evidence is weak, the buyer prices you as cost uncertainty.

This is advisory work. It is not an audit, certification, legal opinion or emissions verification — and every deliverable states that boundary.

How CBAM reaches your P&L

Import friction

The buyer needs a defensible CBAM file. Product classification, installation evidence and embedded-emissions logic decide how your imports are evaluated.

Data friction

If the buyer cannot rely on your data, you get conservative default values, stronger clauses, discount pressure or reduced priority — the difference comes out of your price.

Contract friction

CBAM duties move into supplier clauses: data accuracy, audit rights, notification duties, record retention and liability for unsupported information.

What the review covers

  1. Product scope. Material exposure, CN-code logic and which flows are actually CBAM-covered — before assumptions become obligations.
  2. Installation and production evidence. Site records, production routes and the connection between product and installation data.
  3. Embedded-emissions logic. Sources, methodology support, carbon-price data and the documentation an importer can defend.
  4. Contract and confidentiality controls. What clauses request, what you can prove, and how data is shared without exposing industrial secrets.
  5. Prioritised gap register. What exists, what is missing, who owns each item — graded against the SEMM framework.

The deliverable: a CBAM evidence-readiness map — what the buyer may need, which records exist, which data gaps remain, which claims are weak and which next steps come first, before buyer pressure becomes a commercial deadline.

A concrete example

A steel exporter receives this line in a renewal e-mail: "Your EU importer requires embedded-emissions data at installation level for CBAM." The operation is real; the data exists in five spreadsheets, two systems and one consultant's report. What the buyer receives decides whether the negotiation starts from evidence — or from default values and discounts. That translation is exactly what this review produces.

Questions we hear first

We are not the declarant — is this our problem?

Formally the obligation belongs to the importer. Commercially, the supplier that cannot support the importer's file becomes the friction — and friction is priced.

Do you verify our emissions?

No. Emissions verification is an accredited activity. We review whether your evidence and its documentation would survive the importer's scrutiny — and where it would not.

What does it cost?

Case by case, with a written proposal — depth is driven by product scope and how scattered the records are. No price list, by design.

title: EUDR Evidence Review
custom_excerpt: Origin, geolocation and legality mapped before the buyer asks: traceability files, due-diligence records and the gaps that turn origin claims into market-access risk.
meta_title: EUDR Evidence Review for Brazilian Suppliers | Villanova ESG
meta_description: Advisory review of EUDR evidence: commodity scope, geolocation and origin files, legality records and due-diligence documentation for Brazilian suppliers facing EU buyer traceability requests.
html:
EUDR pressure reaches Brazilian suppliers through buyer questionnaires, onboarding screens and contract discussions — usually before any formal regulatory interaction. The weak point is rarely the commodity. It is the evidence chain behind origin, legality and due diligence. Buyers are asking ahead of the law's application to their own duties.

Advisory review only. Not an audit, certification, legal opinion or guarantee of buyer acceptance.

Three ways origin evidence fails

Declared, not geolocated

Origin is declared, but the declaration cannot be connected to usable geolocation evidence, plot-level data or a traceable file.

Traceable, not assessed

Origin data exists, but there is no defensible risk assessment, mitigation logic or due-diligence record structured for buyer review.

Relevant, not board-ready

The evidence affects market access, but it is not organised in a format a CFO, a board or a European procurement team can actually use.

What the review covers

  1. Commodity and product scope. Whether your goods, inputs and supplier flows are connected to EUDR-covered categories — coffee, cocoa, soy, beef, leather, wood, rubber and derived products.
  2. Geolocation and origin evidence. Plot-level information, origin data and whether declarations connect to verifiable files.
  3. Legality records. The documentation chain behind each legality claim, read the way a buyer's due-diligence team reads it.
  4. Due-diligence structure. Risk-assessment logic, mitigation records and data-sharing controls.
  5. Prioritised gap register. Owners, dates and sources per item — graded against the SEMM framework.

The deliverable: an origin-evidence map your commercial team can defend — what is proved, what is declared-but-unproven, and what to fix before the buyer's onboarding screen decides for you.

A concrete example

A coffee exporter receives a buyer portal request: "Provide geolocation coordinates for every plot of origin for shipments after 30 December 2026." The cooperative structure is real, the origin is genuine — but declarations, plots and custody records live in different hands. Whether that becomes a lost account or a renewal depends on the evidence chain, not the coffee.

Questions we hear first

We already have certifications — is that enough?

Certifications help, but EUDR requests are evidence-specific: geolocation, legality and due-diligence records in a usable chain. A certificate that cannot be connected to plots and custody does not answer the portal.

Our buyers have not asked yet — too early?

Buyers are asking ahead of the law. Building the chain under a deadline is the expensive version of the same work.

What does it cost?

Case by case, with a written proposal — driven by commodity scope and supplier-base complexity. No price list, by design.

title: CSDDD & Contract Clause Review
custom_excerpt: What each clause really requests — due-diligence duties, audit rights, data obligations — and what you can prove before signing. Due diligence read as contract risk, not ESG language.
meta_title: CSDDD & Contract Clause Review for EU-Facing Suppliers | Villanova ESG
meta_description: Advisory review of due-diligence and contract clauses for Brazilian suppliers: CSDDD-driven duties, audit rights, warranties, data obligations and termination triggers — against your actual evidence.
html:
European due-diligence law arrives at your desk as contract language: warranties, audit rights, data duties, code-of-conduct annexes, termination triggers. The question is never whether the clause sounds reasonable. It is whether your operation can prove what the clause makes you promise — because an unsupported promise is risk transferred onto you.

This is advisory work — evidence against clauses. It is not legal advice, audit or certification; your counsel remains your counsel.

Where clause risk hides

Warranties without files

"Supplier warrants compliance with…" — signed without a register of what evidence actually supports each warranted claim.

Audit rights without control

Access, records and interviews granted broadly, with no document governance defining what exists, where, and who answers.

Data duties without limits

Continuous data obligations that expose operational detail — with no confidentiality controls or defined scope of sharing.

What the review covers

  1. Clause-by-clause request map. What each clause actually requests in evidence terms — due-diligence duties, reporting, cooperation, retention, liability.
  2. Evidence match. Your records against each request: supported, partially supported, unsupported.
  3. Risk-transfer reading. Which clauses convert regulatory duties (CSDDD and buyer policies) into your commercial liability.
  4. Negotiation support file. What to accept, what to bound, what to evidence first — in language procurement and legal both understand.
  5. Prioritised gap register. Owners and dates per item — graded against the SEMM framework.

The deliverable: a clause-risk map your team takes into the negotiation — every request, every gap, every priority — so the contract reflects what the operation can actually defend.

A concrete example

A metal-parts supplier receives a renewal contract with a new annex: due-diligence cooperation, human-rights and environmental warranties, audit rights "upon reasonable notice", and data duties "as reasonably requested". Signing as-is transfers the buyer's CSDDD exposure downstream. Bounding each clause to evidenced reality — before signature — is what this review prepares.

Questions we hear first

Is this legal advice?

No. Your counsel negotiates the contract. We produce the evidence reading — what you can prove — that makes your counsel's position defensible.

CSDDD keeps changing — is this premature?

The duties reach you through buyer contracts regardless of transposition timing. The clause on your desk is already the law that binds you.

What does it cost?

Case by case, with a written proposal — driven by contract volume and evidence complexity. No price list, by design.

A contract with new clauses on the table? Send the clause as it arrived — we reply with the priority risks and the recommended next step, within 1 business day.

title: Product Data & DPP Review
custom_excerpt: The data burden of the Digital Product Passport, structured at source: product records, material composition, circularity data and the controls that keep industrial secrets safe.
meta_title: Product Data & DPP Review for EU-Facing Suppliers | Villanova ESG
meta_description: Advisory review of product data for the EU Digital Product Passport and buyer data requests: composition, circularity, traceability records and confidentiality controls for Brazilian suppliers.
html:
The EU is moving product regulation from declarations to structured, verifiable product data — the Digital Product Passport under the Ecodesign framework. For Brazilian suppliers this lands as buyer spreadsheets, data templates and portal fields: composition, origin, circularity, repairability, recycled content. Whoever cannot fill the fields with defensible data becomes the supply chain's weak link.

This is advisory work. It is not an audit, certification or legal opinion — and every deliverable states that boundary.

Why product data is now commercial risk

Data debt

Every product shipped without structured data is a liability that will be back-filled later, under deadline, at a higher cost — or lost with the account.

Buyer-readability

Data that exists but cannot be transferred into the buyer's template is treated as missing. Format is part of the evidence.

Industrial secrets

DPP requests can expose composition and process detail. Sharing without confidentiality controls converts compliance into competitive risk.

What the review covers

  1. Product-data exposure map. Which products, buyers and templates create data duties now — and which are coming with the DPP rollout.
  2. Record review. Composition, material, circularity and traceability records against what the buyer's template actually asks.
  3. Gap and format register. What exists, what is missing, what exists-but-is-not-transferable — with owners and dates.
  4. Confidentiality controls. What to share, in which format, under which limits — so data duties do not expose industrial secrets.
  5. Structured-at-source plan. The order of work that turns data debt into a reusable product-data file, graded against the SEMM framework.

The deliverable: a product-data readiness map — fields you can answer today, fields you cannot, and the shortest path to a file that answers the next template without a fire drill.

A concrete example

A furniture exporter receives a buyer template with 46 product-data fields — recycled content, wood origin, coating composition, end-of-life instructions. The factory knows the answers; the answers live in purchase orders, supplier e-mails and one engineer's head. Converting that into a template the buyer accepts — without exposing the coating formula — is exactly what this review structures.

Questions we hear first

Is the DPP already mandatory?

The framework is phasing in by product group — but buyer templates are not waiting. The commercial obligation arrives with the request, not the regulation.

Can we refuse sensitive fields?

Often you can bound them — aggregated values, ranges, third-party attestation. That is a controls conversation, and it works better before the first refusal.

What does it cost?

Case by case, with a written proposal — driven by product-line count and data dispersion. No price list, by design.
